INDIRA'S RESPONSE WAS TO GO OVER THE PARTY BOSSES'
ELECTORATE — CONVERTING CONGRESS FROM A FEDERATED MACHINE INTO
THE 1969 SPLIT (CONGRESS-R VS CONGRESS-O) INSTITUTIONALISED A LEFT-OF-CENTRE

groups.heading: OPTIONAL SOURCE DEPTH
items: Under Shastri the Prime Minister's Secretariat (PMO) gained weight — an early sign of executive centralisation that would deepen under Indira.
The 1967 elections shattered one-party dominance: united anti-Congressism, coalition (SVD) governments and
mass defections (nearly 800 legislators crossed floors, 1967–70) destabilised the states.
CAUTION: Indira's response was to go over the party bosses' heads to the

groups.heading: ADVANCED DEBATE
items: electorate — converting Congress from a federated machine into a leader-centred, plebiscitary party.
The 1969 split (Congress-R vs Congress-O) institutionalised a left-of-centre vs right-of-centre
cleavage, with most MPs and the AICC siding with Indira.
Bank nationalisation (1969) and the abolition of privy purses (1971) were populist-radical measures that isolated the Syndicate and rallied the poor.

groups.heading: LEGACY / NUANCE
items: The 1971 "Garibi Hatao" landslide (Congress-R, 352/518) rested on a direct appeal to
a coalition of the poor and disadvantaged, delinking national from state voting.
The Bangladesh war (1971) victory made Indira dominant, and Pokhran-I (1974) projected strategic strength.
CAUTION: But personalisation weakened the party organisation and institutional checks —
